name: News Media
description: Iran’s news media combine news agencies, national newspapers, local reporting, and specialist publications. Their history reflects both professional innovation and recurring restrictions on editorial freedom, while institutional affiliation and access conditions shape how their reporting should be interpreted.

seo.title: News Media in Iran: Institutions, History and Reading Sources
seo.description: Understand Iranian news agencies and newspapers, their historical development, editorial constraints, and the limits of available evidence.

content.heading: Reading a layered news landscape
content.content:
A useful introduction to Iranian news begins with the institution behind a report. An agency, a newspaper, and an archive perform different functions, even when their material appears together in an online search. Institutional boundaries can also overlap: the Organization of Asia-Pacific News Agencies, or OANA, describes IRNA, the Islamic Republic News Agency, as owning a press institute that publishes newspapers. Its profile of Mehr places that agency and the English-language Tehran Times within the same media group. These examples show why a website’s format alone cannot establish its organizational independence. [s2][s3]

For an international reader, the practical question is therefore more precise than whether a story comes from 'Iranian media.' Identify the named publisher, the original speaker or document, and whether the item presents reporting, an interview, or editorial interpretation. Shared institutional connections are relevant context; they do not, by themselves, establish whether a particular factual statement is correct. [s2][s3]

content.heading: Expansion and restriction
content.content:
The revolution of 1978–79 produced an opening for competing publications, followed by closures and consolidation. Historian Hossein Shahidi describes the closure of Ayandegan and the state takeover of Ettelaat and Kayhan by August 1979. His account also traces successive post-revolution press laws and restrictions. This history helps explain why the survival of a newspaper title should not be mistaken for continuity of ownership or editorial purpose. [s1]

Historical news can be explored through the University of Manchester Library’s Nashriyah collection. It brings together publications from the premiership of Mohammad Mossadegh and the coup against his government, the revolution, and the later reform period associated with President Mohammad Khatami. The collection offers evidence of what particular publications printed at particular moments; it is not a representative survey of everything Iranians read or believed. [s4]

content.heading: Conditions behind the published story
content.content:
Restrictions operate through more than formal newspaper bans. In its report on the first half of 2025, the Defending Free Flow of Information organization documented threatening calls, pressure to remove posts, interference with journalists’ communications, and judicial proceedings. These are findings from an organization monitoring press suppression, rather than a government statistical census. They provide evidence of reporting constraints without measuring the entire media economy. [s5]

Access conditions can also change abruptly. Reporters Without Borders, an international press-freedom organization, reported a communications blackout in January 2026, difficulty contacting independent newsrooms, and the suspension of Ham-Mihan. Its account describes that episode; it does not establish which websites or print editions were operating at the October research cutoff. A temporarily unreachable website cannot alone prove permanent closure. [s6]

content.heading: Following the right branch
content.content:
The pages below separate institutions that gather and distribute news from newspapers with their own editions and editorial identities. National newspapers are particularly useful for studying changes in public argument over time, while agency profiles help identify the institutional origin of frequently repeated reports. Historical archives support both approaches, provided the publication date and original context remain visible. [s2][s3][s4]

This introduction is strongest on agencies, national newspapers, and documented reporting restrictions. It does not yet provide an adequately verified account of provincial, specialist, economic, or technology journalism. Those branches require their own sources rather than assumptions drawn from Tehran’s national press.

name: Iranian News Agencies
description: Iranian news agencies include institutions with different histories, publishing relationships, and language services. IRNA, Mehr, and the Iranian Students’ News Agency illustrate parts of this landscape, but their directory descriptions and historical records do not constitute a complete current register.

seo.title: Iranian News Agencies: IRNA, Mehr and ISNA
seo.description: An evidence-based introduction to selected Iranian news agencies, their publishing connections, language services, and verification limits.

content.heading: Start with the agency’s identity
content.content:
Agency names often travel with a report into other publications. Understanding the institution named in that attribution is a useful first step, but a directory profile cannot substitute for checking the underlying report. The Organization of Asia-Pacific News Agencies, or OANA, provides institutional profiles for IRNA and Mehr that establish their names and describe parts of their publishing operations. These are institutional descriptions rather than independent assessments of editorial performance. [s1][s2]

IRNA stands for Islamic Republic News Agency. OANA traces its origins to Pars News Agency in 1934 and dates its renaming to 1982. Its profile also describes newspaper publishing through the Iran Cultural and Press Institute. The important distinction is between the agency and the publications associated with it: a newspaper bearing a related institutional identity is still a particular publication, with its own edition and content. [s1]

content.heading: Connections between agencies and newspapers
content.content:
Mehr provides another example of an agency connected to a newspaper. OANA’s profile describes Mehr Media Group as comprising Mehr News Agency and the Tehran Times. That documented connection helps readers recognize that apparently separate publication brands can belong to a shared organizational structure. The profile’s promotional claims about reach should not be treated as audited audience evidence. [s2]

These examples also caution against treating 'news agency' and 'newspaper' as mutually exclusive corporate categories. The relevant questions concern the specific organization and product: who issued the original item, which publication reproduced it, and whether additional reporting was added. The verified profiles support the existence of publishing connections; they do not establish the complete editorial decision-making process inside either group. [s1][s2]

content.heading: English-language material and its limits
content.content:
The Iranian Students’ News Agency is commonly abbreviated ISNA. A research abstract by Mohammad Kamel and Hadi Sadoghi-Yazdi describes an English-language news corpus assembled from ISNA material. This establishes that English ISNA reporting was available for that research, rather than demonstrating that its English output represented the full Persian service. Only the abstract was inspected here; detailed corpus findings are therefore outside this page’s evidence base. [s3]

An English article is best approached as a specific editorial product. Readers should record its date, attributed speaker, and original publisher, and avoid assuming equivalence with another language edition unless both versions have been checked. The ISNA research identifies a language-specific corpus, while OANA separately identifies agency websites and institutional connections. Neither source supplies a comprehensive comparison of translated and original output. [s1][s2][s3]

content.heading: A selective introduction
content.content:
Availability is another dimension of the agency landscape. In its January 2026 reporting on Iran’s communications blackout, Reporters Without Borders noted that some state-aligned information services remained accessible while independent newsrooms were difficult to reach. This is evidence about unequal access during a documented episode, rather than a permanent classification of every agency’s availability or reliability. [s4]

The profiles here are deliberately selective. A publication-ready national overview also requires verified histories, institutional affiliations, and current operating information for other major agencies, including Fars and Tasnim. Their omission from the detailed profiles should not be read as a judgment about their importance.

name: National Newspapers
description: Iran’s national newspapers preserve a record of changing journalistic styles, institutional relationships, and political debate. Their titles must be read in historical context because ownership, editorial direction, and permission to publish have changed over time.

seo.title: National Newspapers in Iran: Titles, History and Archives
seo.description: Explore selected Iranian national newspapers, historical changes in ownership and editorial identity, and sources for reading original editions.

content.heading: Newspapers as institutions and historical records
content.content:
Iran’s national newspaper history is more than a succession of titles. It includes competition over journalistic style, changes in ownership, and disputes over what could be published. Kayhan illustrates the importance of period: Encyclopaedia Iranica describes its development under Mostafa Mesbahzadeh before the revolution and its later publication under the patronage of the Islamic Republic’s supreme leader. A title’s longevity therefore cannot establish an unchanged editorial identity. [s1]

The Tehran Kayhan must also be distinguished from Kayhan of London. Iranica identifies the latter as a separate weekly founded in exile in 1984. Confusing the two would merge publications with different institutional histories. This distinction matters when searching archives, identifying an editorial, or attributing a contemporary statement. [s1]

content.heading: Ayandegan and competition over reporting
content.content:
Ayandegan first appeared in Tehran on 16 December 1967. Its founders sought a morning newspaper with a more substantial approach to reporting and commentary, challenging the established position of Ettelaat and Kayhan. Iranica’s account emphasizes both its innovations and the political controls within which it worked. Describing its liberalizing ambitions does not imply that it operated in an unrestricted press system. [s2]

The same account distinguishes influence from circulation: Ayandegan did not match the two large evening papers in sales, yet carried weight among political elites. It is a useful historical example of why circulation alone cannot measure a newspaper’s role in public debate. Its subsequent closure belongs to the broader contraction of the press after the revolution. [s2][s3]

content.heading: Revolution and later publishing arrangements
content.content:
The revolutionary opening did not produce a lasting unrestricted newspaper market. Hossein Shahidi’s historical account describes closures, including Ayandegan, and the state takeover of Ettelaat and Kayhan by August 1979. It also records the emergence of publications associated with competing political actors. A newspaper’s institutional position must consequently be located in time rather than projected backward or forward from a single period. [s3]

The daily Iran represents a different publishing connection. Iranica dates its establishment to January 1995 and identifies it as a newspaper published by IRNA, the Islamic Republic News Agency. This distinguishes Iran, the newspaper title, from both the country and the agency itself. The historical account explains its association with government perspectives, but cannot establish its precise editorial arrangements at the present cutoff. [s4]

content.heading: Recent restrictions need dated descriptions
content.content: Reporters Without Borders reported that Ham-Mihan was suspended in January 2026 and that several newspaper websites were inaccessible from abroad during the communications blackout. These are dated findings. They should not be expanded into a claim that all affected newspapers permanently ceased printing or remained inaccessible throughout the year. Current operating status requires later, publication-specific evidence. [s5]

content.heading: Reading original editions
content.content:
For historical exploration, the University of Manchester Library’s Nashriyah collection offers digitized newspapers and periodicals from several major political turning points. Reading an original edition helps preserve the relationship between headlines, commentary, advertisements, and surrounding reports. The library describes a selected collection, so gaps in its holdings should not be interpreted as proof that a title or issue never existed. [s6]

The most useful reading habit is to retain the publication name and issue date alongside every excerpt. Compare the article’s wording with its attributed source, and separate an editorial position from a reported event. National newspapers can illuminate competing interpretations of Iranian history without any single title standing for the country as a whole. [s1][s2][s6]
